newsitem.title: USA: Fed seen keeping rates steady in July - Fed alumni.
newsitem.headline: Fed seen keeping rates steady in July - Fed alumni.

text.p: The Federal Reserve is likely to leave interest rates unchanged in July as the economy appears to be cooling from torrid first quarter growth levels while inflation remains absent, former Fed officials said.
"I doubt the Fed will tighten (monetary policy) next week ... I think they will leave rates unchanged," said Lyle Gramley, a former member of the Fed's Board of Governors.

"First because there aren't any concrete signs of any upturn ...yet in growth and second because ... inflation remains very tranquil," added Gramley, currently a consulting economist for the Mortgage Bankers Association.
The Fed's policy-setting body, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), will meet next on July 1 and 2 to deliberate on interest rates.
The central bank last changed monetary policy on March 25, when it raised the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent. The Fed left rates unchanged at the May 20 meeting of the FOMC.

Pundits said the current rosy economic scenario -- in which inflationary threats are nowhere to be found -- also makes tightening monetary policy in July a tough political decision for the Federal Reserve.

"I don't expect any increases in rates in this FOMC ... I think the political situation may be such that they will pass for political reasons," said Preston Martin, a former vice chairman at the Federal Reserve.
The Fed faced harsh criticism from both Democrats and Republicans alike after it decided to raise rates in March at a time when inflation already appeared tame.

Several prominent Fed members, however, have publicly rebuffed any political criticism, praising the Fed's independence and saying the central bank has to be able to respond to inflationary pressures before they take root in the economy.

At the current stage, however, the U.S. economy looks like a central banker's nirvana -- there are few wage pressures despite tight labor markets, consumer demand is cooling after sizzling early 1997 levels, and inflation is numb.

"I don't see any major imbalances in the economy. So basically ... there's no reason for the Fed to hit the brakes because the inflationary pressures are clearly under control," said Robert Heller, a former Fed governor.

"There is certainly nothing right now on the horizon that would make me think that (Fed) action is needed," added Heller, currently an executive vice president at the San Francisco-based firm Fair Isaac & Co.

Also, Fed watchers said, current monetary policy is seen as slightly restrictive, with the federal funds rate at 5.50 percent and the consumer price index running around an annual rate of 2.5 percent.
But central bank alumni warned that this blissful scenario is not likely to continue throughout the year, adding that they believe the Fed might have to tighten interest rates sometime later in 1997.
They said one of the potential bottlenecks is likely to stem from an extremely tight labor market.

"When you look at aggregate demand growth, it is still ahead of aggregate supply growth. So I think the Fed is going to have to act (in the future)," said Martin, who is now the chairman of HomeVest Financial Services Inc.
"I don't expect an increase in rates in this FOMC (in July), but I certainly expect them in the future," he added.
On average, Fed watchers said they expect consumers to start spending again in the third quarter of the year, which in turn is expected to fuel economic growth.

If true, that is likely to bring U.S. Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth to the vicinity of 3.0 percent in the third quarter of the year against forecasts of a 2.0 percent growth in the second quarter.
GDP grew by 5.9 percent in the first three months of 1997.
Experts said extremely high levels of consumer confidence are seen as another factor underpinning the expected third quarter rebound in consumption.
Consumer confidence as measured by the Conference Board jumped to 129.6 in June, the highest level since August 1969.
"We have very high levels of consumer confidence, which are well justified by what's happening in both labor markets and financial markets," Gramley said.
"Labor markets are creating jobs at a very rapid pace.

"In financial markets, stock prices are booming, making consumers wealthy, and interest rates on long-term securities are actually lower now than they were in the beginning of this recovery," he added.
